title: Zero Trust for digital ID wallets: verify the holder, the device and the issuer every time
sum: A digital identity wallet concentrates a person's most valuable credentials on one phone. Zero Trust gives a simple rule for protecting it: never accept a presentation because of where it came from, and verify the holder, the device, the issuer and the relying party on every transaction.

sources.name: EUDI Wallet - Architecture and Reference Framework

body: In brief. NIST SP 800-207 describes Zero Trust as removing implicit trust and evaluating every access request. Applied to identity wallets, that means four checks on every presentation: the holder is the rightful user, the wallet and device are genuine and healthy, the credential is valid and unrevoked, and the relying party is who it claims to be and is entitled to ask.
Why wallets need Zero Trust thinking

With EU Member States due to offer European Digital Identity Wallets by 24 December 2026, and national wallet programs growing elsewhere, more high-value transactions will start with a wallet presentation. That makes the wallet an attractive target: stolen phones, malware that drives the wallet app, cloned or emulated wallets, fake relying parties that over-collect data, and credentials that should have been revoked.
Four checks on every presentation

HolderLocal user authentication and, for high-risk actions, a fresh biometric or PIN
Every presentation
Wallet and deviceWallet attestation, key protection in secure hardware, device integrity signals
Every presentation
Issuer and credentialIssuer signature, trust list membership, revocation or status check
Every presentation
Relying partyAuthenticated relying party and limits on which attributes it may request
Every request

The EUDI Architecture and Reference Framework already builds in several of these: wallet attestations, relying party authentication and registration, and selective disclosure so the holder shares only the attributes needed.
Policy, not perimeter

In a Zero Trust design, a policy decision point evaluates each request using all available signals, and enforcement points apply the decision. For a wallet ecosystem that means the issuer, the wallet provider and each relying party apply their own checks, and none of them assumes that an earlier step was enough. A payment approved with a wallet credential at 9:00 does not make a new payee at 9:05 safe.
What issuers, wallet providers and relying parties should do

Issuers

Bind credentials to hardware-protected keys and keep status services fast and available.

Wallet providers

Harden the app, attest wallet instances and detect tampering and remote control.

Relying parties

Authenticate to the wallet, request minimum data and verify signatures and status every time.

Everyone

Log decisions, monitor for anomalies and plan for key and algorithm changes, including post-quantum.

Digital ID Wallet supports hardware-protected credentials and selective disclosure. Zero Trust Gateway Appliance checks identity, device health and policy on every request, and Device Intelligence adds live device risk to each presentation.

title: Wallet-based onboarding for banks: cutting KYC fraud while meeting AML rules
sum: Digital identity wallets let customers share verified identity data instead of photographing documents. For banks, that can cut document fraud and drop-off at onboarding - if the wallet flow is built into customer due diligence, not bolted on beside it.
body: In brief. Under eIDAS 2.0, EU Member States must offer at least one European Digital Identity Wallet by 24 December 2026, and regulated sectors such as banking are required to accept it for authentication by late 2027. The EU AML Regulation applies from 10 July 2027. Banks that design wallet onboarding now can use verified identity data to reduce document fraud while keeping customer due diligence complete and auditable.
Why document-based eKYC is under pressure

Remote onboarding today usually means a photo of an ID document, a selfie and a liveness check. Each step is now a target: forged and template-generated documents, injected camera feeds and deepfaked faces. A wallet changes the starting point. Instead of a picture of a document, the bank receives identity attributes signed by the issuer, which it can verify cryptographically.
What the AML view requires

The FATF's Guidance on Digital Identity sets out a risk-based approach: banks should understand the assurance level of a digital ID system and rely on it for customer due diligence in proportion to that assurance. A wallet presentation can establish who the customer is. It does not by itself answer the other due diligence questions.

Identity

Verified attributes from the wallet, checked against the issuer's signature and status.

Purpose and nature

Expected use of the account, still collected by the bank.

Ownership and control

Beneficial ownership for legal entities and representatives.

Screening and monitoring

Sanctions, PEP and adverse media screening, then ongoing transaction monitoring.
A wallet onboarding flow that holds up

1Request

The bank asks only for the attributes it needs, as an authenticated relying party.

2Verify

Check the issuer signature, the credential status and that the wallet is genuine.

3Bind

Confirm the person presenting is the holder, using the wallet's own authentication and, where risk requires, a biometric match.

4Complete CDD

Add purpose, screening and risk rating, then record the evidence for audit.
Where fraud still gets in

Coached customers

A genuine person opens an account for a fraudster, so mule detection still matters.

Compromised phones

Remote-access malware can steer a real wallet session; device risk scoring still applies.

Fallback paths

If document-based onboarding stays open beside the wallet, attackers will choose it.

Over-collection

Asking for more attributes than needed creates privacy risk without reducing fraud.
How SAVIS helps

Digital ID Wallet supports issuing and presenting verifiable credentials. TrustCA eKYC Biometric and SAVIS TrustOnboard cover biometric binding and document-based fallback, while Device Intelligence checks the phone behind each session.

title: Adaptive mobile app defense: from RASP to fleet-wide intelligence
sum: Mobile apps are now the front door to banks and public services. Protecting them takes more than static checks: runtime defense, device trust, context-aware APIs and intelligence that sees attacks across the whole app population.

sources.name: NIST FIPS 203 - Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism Standard

body: In brief. Attackers now combine classic hooking, debugging and repackaging with AI-assisted automation and coordinated campaigns across thousands of devices. Defending a banking or government app means four connected layers: runtime defense inside the app, device trust and secure communications, threat intelligence across the fleet, and automated response tied to the back end.
Why the mobile endpoint is the new battleground
Banking, wallet and government apps handle credentials, identity records and high-value transactions. The threats have changed:

Runtime exploitation

Dynamic instrumentation, hooking, debugging, code injection and repackaging to bypass controls.

AI-assisted attacks

Tools that speed up reverse engineering and generate endless variations of malicious behavior.

Device compromise

Malware and hostile operating environments that undermine authentication and expose transactions.

API abuse

Weak client authentication, session integrity or transaction authorization exploited to automate fraud.

Coordinated campaigns

Attacks spread across many devices and sessions, hard to read one device at a time.

Cryptographic risk

Long-lived sensitive data that needs a path to quantum-resistant protection.
Four layers that work together

Runtime defenseRoot and jailbreak, integrity, anti-debugging, hooking and injection detection
Inside the app
Device trust and secure communicationsTrust scoring, TLS and certificate pinning, protected keys, white-box cryptography, crypto agility
Device and channel
Fleet-wide intelligenceEvent streaming, anomaly detection, cross-device correlation, campaign clustering
Back end
Automated responseStep-up, restrict, re-authorize, quarantine, alert and recover
Policy
Adaptive, not just rule-based

Classic RASP relies on fixed rules and fixed responses. An adaptive approach correlates several signals, adjusts risk thresholds and updates policies centrally as new attack patterns appear. The goal is to catch more attacks while interrupting fewer genuine customers, with responses graded by severity instead of a single block-or-allow switch.
Device trust should shape every sensitive decision

1Trusted session

Normal transaction workflow.

2Elevated risk

Additional verification before the payment or change.

3High risk

Sensitive operations restricted, session quarantined, SOC alerted.

Trust scores add to identity verification and authorization; they do not replace them. The same context can protect APIs: app integrity, device trust, session authenticity, transaction sensitivity and replay or automation indicators are evaluated on each sensitive request, alongside API gateways and firewalls.
See the campaign, not only the incident

One rooted phone is an incident. Hundreds of devices with the same hooking framework hitting the same payment API in an hour is a campaign. Streaming telemetry from every protected install, then applying anomaly detection, clustering and statistical baselines, lets security teams see coordinated abuse that is invisible on a single device. Federated learning can improve detection across deployments while keeping sensitive data local and subject to each customer's authorization.
Recover safely, and prepare for post-quantum

When a compromised state is detected, controlled recovery matters as much as detection: revoke the session, require fresh authentication or device verification, disable high-risk functions temporarily, then restore access after reassessment. On the channel side, a crypto-agile design with TLS, certificate validation and protected key storage can adopt hybrid and post-quantum key establishment, such as ML-KEM under NIST FIPS 203, in validated configurations.
Where it applies

Mobile banking and payments

Protect authorization, detect manipulated apps and compromised devices, strengthen session integrity.

Wallets, fintech and trading

Protect keys and credentials, stop tampering and client automation, watch API access patterns.

Digital identity and eKYC

Protect the capture path and communications around identity checks; liveness and deepfake detection stay separate controls.

Government services

Protect citizen identity and service apps with integrity, controlled access and visibility of coordinated threats.
Standards and regulation

These controls map to OWASP MASVS, MASTG and the API Security Top 10, PCI DSS v4.0.1, DORA, NIST CSF 2.0 and ISO/IEC 27001. They also support regional rules: SBV Circulars 50/2024/TT-NHNN and 77/2025/TT-NHNN in Vietnam, DORA and PSD2/PSD3 in the EU, BSP Circulars 1213-1215 under AFASA in the Philippines, MAS technology risk guidelines in Singapore, BNM RMiT in Malaysia, the Scams Prevention Framework and APRA CPS 234 in Australia, the Privacy Act 2020 in New Zealand, SAMA, CBUAE and Central Bank of Egypt rules and data protection laws in the Middle East and North Africa, the CBN cybersecurity framework in Nigeria, central bank cybersecurity rules in Brazil, Peru and Chile, and NIST, FFIEC and NYDFS requirements in the United States. Compliance of a full application still depends on its complete implementation and processes.

RASP+ protects the app at runtime with adaptive detection and graded responses. TrustShield adds device trust scoring, context-aware API protection, fleet-wide intelligence and automated response. Device Intelligence and Fraud Prevention & Risk Management bring device and session risk into each transaction decision.

title: Device fingerprinting vs. device intelligence: what banks actually need to know about a device
sum: A device fingerprint tells you whether you have seen this phone before. Device intelligence tells you whether you should trust what is happening on it right now. Banks need both, and they need to know the difference.

sources.name: EDPB - Guidelines 2/2023 on the technical scope of Art. 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive
ICO - Our response to Google's policy change on fingerprinting (December 2024)

body: In brief. Fingerprinting answers one question: is this the same device as before? That is useful, but fraudsters now work from real phones, real customers and real sessions. Device intelligence adds the questions that matter at the moment of a payment: is the device tampered with, emulated, remotely controlled or part of a device farm?
Two different questions

Device fingerprinting

Builds a stable identifier from hardware, software and configuration attributes so a returning device can be recognized.

Device intelligence

Scores the device and session in real time: integrity, environment, behavior and links to other accounts.

Typical use of a fingerprint

Remember trusted devices, spot new-device logins, link accounts that share a device.

Typical use of intelligence

Decide whether to allow, step up, delay or block this login or payment right now.
Why a fingerprint alone is no longer enough

Many of today's losses happen on the customer's own, already trusted phone. In remote-access and social-engineering scams, the fingerprint matches perfectly because the device is genuine. What changed is the context: a screen-sharing tool is running, Accessibility services are driving the app, or the session behaves unlike the customer's usual pattern. A stable identifier cannot see that.

Fingerprints also drift. Operating system updates, browser changes and privacy features alter attributes, so a pure fingerprint either breaks for genuine customers or is tuned so loosely that it groups unrelated devices.
What device intelligence adds

1Integrity

Root or jailbreak, hooking frameworks, repackaged apps and debuggers.

2Environment

Emulators, virtual devices, app cloners and device farms.

3Live threats

Remote-access tools, screen capture, overlay and Accessibility abuse during the session.

4Links

How many accounts, identities and payees this device has touched, and how fast.
Privacy and consent are part of the design

Regulators treat fingerprinting as a privacy matter. In Europe, the EDPB's guidelines on Article 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive (version 2.0, adopted in October 2024) explain that the rule on accessing information stored on a device is not limited to cookies and covers fingerprinting. In the UK, the ICO publicly criticized the use of fingerprinting for advertising in December 2024. For banks, the defensible position is clear purpose limitation: device signals collected for security and fraud prevention, documented in the privacy notice, kept for a defined period and never reused for marketing.
A practical checklist for banks

Separate the two

Use the fingerprint to recognize devices and intelligence to decide risk.

Score every sensitive action

Login, payee change, limit change and payment, not just onboarding.

Explain decisions

Record which device signals drove each step-up or block.

Limit data

Collect what fraud prevention needs, document the legal basis and set retention.

Device Fingerprint SDK recognizes the device behind each login or payment. Device Intelligence scores device and session risk in real time, and Fraud Prevention & Risk Management turns those signals into explainable decisions with audit trails.
